Dermatology · published research

Acne vulgaris

Selected blue, red, and near-infrared protocols reduced inflammatory acne lesions in some controlled studies. Results for non-inflammatory lesions and longer-term control are less consistent, and light protocols are not interchangeable.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Selected blue, red, and near-infrared protocols reduced inflammatory acne lesions in some controlled studies. Results for non-inflammatory lesions and longer-term control are less consistent, and light protocols are not interchangeable.

Summary of the Evidence

The acne category contains 52 publications: 41 human primary reports, about 40 identifiable cohorts after accounting for a known extension, seven reviews or commentaries, one mouse study, and three laboratory-only studies. Two human reports also include laboratory work. The category includes photodynamic therapy and higher-energy or thermal light procedures as well as PBM, so the total is not a count of equivalent PBM trials. Reviews also reuse primary studies.

Human and clinical evidence

Human studies use split-face comparisons, randomized designs, and uncontrolled treatment series. In a 40-person split-face comparison, eight sessions of continuous 808 nm near-infrared laser twice weekly were compared with topical erythromycin on the other side of the face. Both sides improved, and the authors reported greater improvement on the laser-treated side, with follow-up observations to three months (Ashmawy et al. 2024). A later open-label randomized home-device study of 23 participants compared a combined red-and-blue device with blue light alone and reported reductions in inflammatory lesions in both groups; its open-label design and size limit comparisons between devices (Friedmann et al. 2026). A review pooling red-light trials did not find statistically significant pooled changes for inflammatory or non-inflammatory lesions, underscoring that results depend on which studies and protocols are combined (Wu et al. 2021).

Animal evidence

One mouse study used a Propionibacterium acnes-related model to examine inflammatory responses under different light conditions.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

Three publications are classified as laboratory-only studies, with two additional human papers including laboratory assays. These reports examine processes such as bacterial response, sebocyte activity, or inflammatory signaling. Results under cell-culture exposure do not determine the clinical effect of a device on acne.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Protocols include blue visible light, red visible light, combinations of red and blue, and 808 nm near-infrared laser light. The 808 nm split-face study used eight sessions over four weeks; home-device studies use different wavelengths and daily schedules. Fluence, irradiance, treatment area, device contact, and follow-up vary, so results should be linked to the specific protocol studied. No single optimal wavelength or dose is established.

Interpretation

Some controlled studies report short-term reductions in inflammatory lesions, while non-inflammatory results and pooled red-light estimates are less consistent. The evidence supports outcome-specific conclusions for particular devices and schedules rather than a general claim that all light-based acne treatments work equally well.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow-to-moderate for short-term reduction in inflammatory lesions with selected light protocols Low for non-inflammatory lesions and longer-term control
Publications and records52 articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Several controlled studies report short-term reductions in inflammatory lesions, including a split-face comparison with topical erythromycin. However, small trials use different wavelengths and schedules, and a red-light meta-analysis did not find significant pooled improvement. Non-inflammatory outcomes are less consistent. A larger sham-controlled trial with standardized lesion counts and follow-up after treatment would strengthen these outcome-specific estimates.
